chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ibn Abi Nasr from Hammad ibn 'Uthman from Muhammad ibn Abi al-Subbah said:

I said to Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him): 'My mother gave me a gift of her share in a house. I told her that the judges do not validate this type of gift, but write it as a sale.' She said: 'Do what seems good to you and whatever you deem permissible for yourself.' I became secure (from being challenged), but some of the heirs wanted to make me swear an oath that I had paid her the price, although I had not paid her anything. What do you think? He said, 'Swear to them.'
Then he said: Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub from Muhammad ibn al-Faraj from Ali ibn Ma'bad said: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Ibrahim ibn Muhammad wrote to him in the year 231 AH:

He asked him about a man who died leaving a wife, sons, and daughters, and left them a slave whom he had endowed (waqf) for them for ten years, after which he would be free. Is it permissible for these heirs to sell this slave if they are in need, as I have described to you? May God be my ransom, he wrote back (peace be upon him): 'Do not sell him until the time limit he specified has passed, unless they are in need of it, in which case it is permissible for them.'
ai.seo_question: What is the juristic ruling on selling an endowed slave or property designated for heirs before the specified time period expires?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the pragmatic application of *hiyal* (legal stratagems) in Shia jurisprudence to preserve family wealth, specifically validating the conversion of a gift into a sale to prevent heirs from reclaiming it. The second ruling clarifies the conditions under which a temporary *waqf* (endowment) of a slave can be liquidated for the heirs' benefit, balancing the donor's intent with the heirs' financial necessity. These rulings highlight the flexibility of Shia legal theory in adapting fixed religious obligations to dynamic socio-economic realities.
